chapters.title: Diagnose, Don't Blame: Find the Missing Piece in a Habit
chapters.hook: It is Sunday night, and the habit you swore to start on Monday has failed again. You are about to call yourself lazy and promise to try harder. What if a missing piece is the problem, not you?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a habit that keeps failing proves they are lazy and need more discipline. Actually, a failed habit means one of three parts is missing, because a behavior only happens when desire, ability, and a cue all meet at once.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit keeps failing, ask which of three things is missing instead of calling yourself lazy.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one habit you keep missing, and on a sticky note write which part is weak: the cue, the ease, or the wish. Do it tonight, because naming the gap works better than blaming yourself.

memorableLines.text: Diagnose, don't blame: a failed habit is a missing piece, not a flawed you.

breakdown.fastRead:
It is nearly midnight, and Tomás has skipped his back stretches for the fourth night in a row. His back aches, so he knows he wants to feel better. He tells himself he is lazy and swears he will try harder tomorrow. That feels honest, because he made a plan and did not follow it. But calling himself lazy gives him nothing to fix.

BJ Fogg, who studies behavior, built a plain tool called the Behavior Model. It says an action happens only when three things meet at the same moment. You need the desire to do it, which he calls motivation. You need the ability, meaning it is easy enough for your time and energy. And you need a prompt, which is a cue that tells you to do it right now. If one is missing, nothing happens, and the missing piece is never your character. So he says to check the prompt first, then the ease, and look at desire last.

Tomás's aching back proves his desire is fine. But no moment tells him to stretch, and his plan takes twenty minutes. So he leaves the mat by his bed, where seeing it is his cue, and cuts the plan to one stretch. You can stop short of fixing every miss, because sometimes you do not truly want the habit, and letting it go is fine. When a habit keeps failing, look for the missing piece before you call yourself lazy.

breakdown.fullRead:
It is nearly midnight, and Tomás has skipped his back stretches for the fourth night in a row. His back aches, so he knows he wants to feel better. He has a mat and a plan, yet the evening slipped away again. He tells himself he is lazy and swears he will try harder tomorrow. But that promise is about to fail the same way the last three did.

Calling himself lazy feels honest, because he made a plan and did not follow it. The plan was clear and the result was nothing, so the blame seems to land on him. Everyone around him says the same thing: push through, stay disciplined, want it more. So the idea sounds like plain common sense, and it is hard to argue with when he is tired and alone at midnight.

The trouble is that blame feels like a fix but changes nothing. Tomorrow night Tomás will have the same evening, the same tired body, and the same lack of a moment to start. Only now he also feels worse about himself, which makes the habit harder to face. Blame also points at the one thing nobody can change by Tuesday: who he is. A person who feels like a failure does not want to look at the thing that made them feel that way. So the stretches slip further away, and each miss seems to prove he really is lazy.

BJ Fogg, who studies behavior, offers a better way to look. He does not treat a missed habit as a flaw in the person. An action is something that happens in a moment, not a trait you carry around. His Behavior Model is a plain way to see why any action happens or does not. It says a behavior happens only when three things meet at the same moment. If even one is missing, nothing happens, and that holds for everybody, whether the action is a stretch, a phone call, or a glass of water.

The first part is motivation, which is your desire to do the thing. The second is ability, which means the action is easy enough for your time, energy, and effort right now. The third is a prompt, which is a cue that tells you to do it now. A text buzzing on your phone is a prompt, and so is a kettle whistling. Any one of them can be missing alone. A person may badly want to read more and have the book on the table, but nothing says now, so the evening goes to the phone. Another has the book and a nudge, but no real wish to read, so nothing happens either. The cue is the part people forget most, because they assume wanting is enough.

Because there are three parts, a failed habit has three places to look, and none of them is your character. Fogg says to check them in a set order. Ask first whether there is a prompt, a clear moment that tells you to start. Then ask whether the habit is easy enough to do on a tired day. Look at desire last, because desire comes and goes, so it is the weakest thing to lean on. Most of the time the fix is a cue or a smaller version, not a stronger wish. That is good news, because a cue can be set up in a minute and a smaller version can be made today. Wanting it harder cannot be built on demand.

Now look at Tomás again. His aching back proves his desire is fine, so motivation is not the problem. But nothing tells him to stretch. He means to do it sometime in the evening, and sometime never arrives. His plan also takes twenty minutes, which is hard to face at midnight. So he leaves the mat by his bed, where seeing it is his cue, and cuts the plan to one stretch. Notice what changed and what did not. His wish is the same and he is just as tired. Only the setup is different. Two pieces were missing, and neither had anything to do with his character. Once he found them, the habit had a fair chance.

Fogg gives this advice bluntly: stop blaming yourself and start reading the habit as a system. It also asks more of you than blame does, because blame ends the thinking and this view starts it. You can stop short of fixing every miss, because sometimes you do not truly want the habit, and letting it go is fine. A habit that still fails with a clear cue and an easy version is telling you something real about what you want.

Back at midnight, Tomás does not need a stern talk with himself. He needs a cue and an easier first step, and both are simple to build. One missed night is not a verdict on him, only a clue about where the habit is weak. The next time one of your own habits fails, do what he did and ask which of the three is missing. When a habit keeps failing, look for the missing piece before you call yourself lazy.

examples.title: The Friday tracker update you keep forgetting
examples.scenario: Dev works at a small design studio, and his team needs the project tracker updated every Friday. He cares about it and it takes five minutes, yet he has missed three weeks. It is 4:30 now, and the tracker is empty again. He opens a note on his phone and starts typing, "I am so disorganized, I must try harder." He has to choose what to do next.
examples.whatToDo: Set a calendar alert for 3:30 every Friday with the tracker link in it, so the cue shows up before he has to remember.
examples.whyItMatters: He wants it done and it is easy, so the missing piece is a cue, not more discipline.

examples.title: The Spanish flashcards that feel too big
examples.scenario: Anneke takes an evening Spanish class and wants to pass the spring exam. She promised herself an hour of flashcards every night, and a phone alarm reminds her at eight. She has skipped five nights, and tonight the huge deck sits on her desk. She is tired, and she is about to tell herself she is hopeless and quit.
examples.whatToDo: Shrink the plan to five cards right after the alarm, and add more only when five feels easy.
examples.whyItMatters: She already has the wish and the cue, so the hour is too big for a tired night.

examples.title: The morning walk you never enjoy
examples.scenario: Imani put her sneakers by the door and set a seven o'clock alarm for a ten-minute walk before work. The walk is short and the cue is clear, yet she keeps skipping it, because she dislikes walking in the cold. This morning she stands at the door in her socks, ready to call herself weak and promise to try harder.
examples.whatToDo: Admit the cue and the ease are fine, then swap the cold walk for something she enjoys, like a dance video at home.
examples.whyItMatters: When the cue and the ease are in place and it still fails, desire is the piece to fix.

questions.prompt: You keep forgetting to take your vitamins with breakfast, and you want to be healthier. You have the bottle and the time. What do you do?
choices: Call yourself forgetful and promise to try a lot harder tomorrow.
Put the bottle next to your coffee mug, where you will see it.
Read articles about vitamins until you feel like taking them more.
questions.explanation: You already have the bottle and the time, so a cue is the missing piece. Promising to try harder blames you, and reading about vitamins works on desire, which comes last.

questions.prompt: A woman keeps missing her Tuesday pottery class. Each week she scolds herself and plans to push harder, but nothing changes. What is the trap?
choices: She reads each miss as weakness, so she never looks for what is missing.
She scolds herself too gently, and a harsher voice would finally get her there.
She picked a hobby that is too hard, and only a new hobby can fix it.
questions.explanation: Reading each miss as weakness leaves nothing to fix. A harsher voice just adds more blame, and switching hobbies skips the check for a missing cue or an easier version.

questions.prompt: A teacher wants to read ten minutes every night. She owns the book and enjoys reading, but nothing tells her when to start. If she only tries harder, what most likely happens?
choices: She grows stronger discipline within a week, since trying harder fixes forgetting.
She reads more only once she finds a stronger reason to love books.
She keeps missing nights, because wanting to read never says when to start.
questions.explanation: With desire and ease already there, the missing piece is a cue. Trying harder does not supply one, and a stronger reason to read works on the piece that was never the problem.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "I keep failing to drink more water. I guess I am just lazy." What is your best reply?
choices: Maybe so, so set a stricter goal and push through it every single day.
Ask what is missing: a cue to drink, an easy way to do it, or a wish.
Tell them to read about the health benefits of water until they care more.
questions.explanation: Asking which of three parts is missing gives your friend something to fix. Setting a stricter goal adds pressure and blame, and reading about benefits works on desire, which comes last.

questions.prompt: A man puts his guitar on a stand by the sofa and plays just five minutes most evenings. Before, it sat in a case and he never touched it. Why did the change work?
choices: The guitar in sight made his wish to play so strong that tiredness stopped mattering.
He built more self-discipline once the guitar was out of its case and on display.
The guitar in view gave him a cue, and five minutes was easy enough to start.
questions.explanation: The stand gave him a cue he could not miss, and five minutes made starting easy. Nothing about his wish or discipline had to change, which is why the fix held.

questions.prompt: You want to call your grandmother every Sunday, and you do care about it. You keep forgetting and remember only on Monday. What do you do?
choices: Set a phone reminder for Sunday at four, when she usually has her tea.
Feel bad every Monday, so the guilt will make you remember next time.
Spend a few minutes each week thinking about how much she means to you.
questions.explanation: You already care, so the missing piece is a cue at a fixed time. Guilt blames you without adding a prompt, and stronger feelings work on desire, which was never the problem.

questions.prompt: A coach tells a player who keeps skipping warm-ups, "You just need to want it more." What is the trap in this advice?
choices: It is too soft, since a stricter team rule and harder practices would fix it.
It starts with desire, when a missing cue or too much effort may be the cause.
It sounds fair, but the real problem is that warm-ups are too dull to keep up.
questions.explanation: Wanting more is the weakest place to start, because desire comes and goes. A missing cue or too much effort is often the cause. A stricter rule adds blame, and dull warm-ups point back at desire.

reviewCards.front: You keep skipping your evening walk, and the thought "I am just lazy" shows up again.
reviewCards.back: Stop and ask which of three things is missing: a cue, an easy enough version, or the wish. Check the cue and the ease first, since they are the usual cause.

reviewCards.front: Why does checking the cue and the ease before the wish work better than trying to want a habit more?
reviewCards.back: Because desire comes and goes, so it is the weakest thing to lean on. A cue or a smaller version can be built today and keeps working on tired days.

reviewCards.front: A behavior happens only when three things meet at once: desire, ability, and ...
reviewCards.back: ... a prompt, which is a cue that tells you to do it right now. If any one of the three is missing, nothing happens.

reviewCards.front: A man put a ten-minute workout on his calendar, felt guilty each time he skipped it, and was no better after a month. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He kept blaming himself and pushing on desire, but never asked what was missing. A cue where he would see it or a two-minute version would have given him something to fix.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do when a habit keeps failing, and why?
reviewCards.back: Ask which of the three is missing, the cue, the ease, or the wish, instead of calling yourself lazy. A missing piece can be fixed, but blame leaves you nothing to work on.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Check for a missing cue first, then for too much effort, and only last for weak desire, before you blame yourself for a failed habit.

ifThenPlans.context: When my sister asks on our weekly call, "Did you do your thing this week?" and I have to say no
ifThenPlans.plan: then I tell her which part was missing, the cue, the ease, or the wish, instead of saying I was lazy.

ifThenPlans.context: When I am brushing my teeth at night and think, "I failed again"
ifThenPlans.plan: then I write one line on the sticky note on the mirror naming the missing piece and one small change to try tomorrow.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, make one fix for the missing piece you named: put what you need where you will trip over it, or shrink the habit to a version under a minute. Then do that version once before bed.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday evening, pick one habit that slipped this week and ask three questions in order: was there a cue, was it easy enough, did I want it. Write down what you find and change one thing.

chapters.title: Sort Many Small Actions, Then Pick One You Want
chapters.hook: Countless small habits could make you feel healthier, and you cannot try them all. Which one deserves your effort, and how can you really tell before you spend weeks on the wrong one?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a better life starts with picking a good habit and pushing through. Actually, you should first list many actions and pick one that works and that you want, because motivation rises and falls and cannot carry a habit.
chapters.keyTakeaway: List many actions that serve one goal, then pick one that works well and that you want.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one wish, like feeling calmer, at the top of a page tonight, then list every small action that could serve it. A long list makes the best one easier to spot.

memorableLines.text: Sort the list first, then pick the action that works and you want.

breakdown.fastRead:
You want to feel healthier, and many habits could get you there. Which one is worth turning into a habit, and how would you know before you waste weeks on the wrong one? Most people just grab the first idea, like running every morning, and promise to push through. That feels right because the first days bring a burst of drive, and it seems the drive will last. But motivation rises and falls like waves, and you cannot count on the next one.

So start with a big wish, which Fogg calls an aspiration, such as feeling healthier. Then write down many small actions that could serve it: a short walk after lunch, a glass of water at your desk, an earlier bedtime. Sort them with Focus Mapping, which means rating each one on how well it would work and how much you want to do it. The best ones are Golden Behaviors, meaning actions that work, that you want, and that you can do.

Back to feeling healthier, the habit worth building is one you find by sorting, because sorting drops actions that need a mood to survive. You can stop short of a perfect chart, because a rough rating on scrap paper is enough. When a wave of motivation does come, spend it on a hard one-time job, like clearing a shelf, not on a heroic daily promise. Sort first, then pick the action that works and that you want.

breakdown.fullRead:
You want to feel healthier, and many habits could get you there. Which one is worth turning into a habit, and how would you know before you waste weeks on the wrong one? Most people just grab the first idea, like running every morning, and promise to push through. It sounds brave, and it sounds like what a serious person does. But you cannot yet tell whether that run is the right action for you or only the first one that came to mind.

That plan feels true for a good reason. On the first day, you are full of drive, and the drive seems to say you are a person who will do this forever. Then a bad night, a long meeting, or a rainy morning arrives, and the drive is gone. Motivation rises and falls in waves, and you cannot count on the next one. When the habit fails, most people blame themselves and think they needed more willpower. The real trouble is the plan, because it needed a wave to show up every single day.

So the first move is to stop picking and start with a wish. Fogg calls a big wish an aspiration, and feeling healthier is one. An aspiration is a fine place to begin, but you cannot do it at three in the afternoon. You cannot just be healthier at your desk. You can only do a specific action, like standing up or drinking water. The wish tells you the direction, and the action is the step you can actually take.

Next, make a long list of actions that could serve the wish. Write down a short walk after lunch, a glass of water at your desk, and an earlier bedtime. Add a piece of fruit with breakfast, and stretching while the kettle boils. Include silly ideas too, and do not judge anything yet. The point is to give yourself many choices, because the first idea may not be the best fit for your life. A long list also makes the best action easier to see, since you can compare it with the others.

Then sort the list with Focus Mapping, which means rating every action on two things. The first is how well it would work for your wish. The second is how much you want to do it. Picture a map where height shows how well an action works and distance across shows how much you want it. Each action lands in its own spot on that map. A dawn run might sit high on the map but far to the left, because it works but you dread it. A magazine about fitness that you enjoy reading might sit far to the right but low, because it does little for your body.

Now look at the top right corner, where the actions both work well and are ones you want. The best of these are Golden Behaviors, meaning actions that work, that you want to do, and that you can do. The third test matters as much as the first two. An action that works and that you love still fails if you cannot fit it into your real week. A walk after lunch might pass all three, because it helps your body, you enjoy the air, and it needs no special gear. Two tests out of three is not enough, so keep sorting until one action passes all of them.

Notice what the sorting did. The dawn run, the one you would have grabbed first, did not survive, because you dread it and it would need a wave of motivation every morning. The walk after lunch survived because it needs no wave to carry it. That is the reason to list many actions and then pick, instead of committing to the first. A good habit is not the most impressive action. It is the one that works and that you want, so it keeps going on days when your mood is low.

Motivation is still worth something when a wave does come, but Fogg points it at a different target. Say you wake up one Saturday burning to get fit. Do not use that fire to swear you will train hard daily, because the fire will fade and the promise will become a weight. Use it for a hard job you do only once. That could be buying walking shoes, clearing the shelf by the door, or finding a safe route around your block. A one-time job needs the wave only once, and afterward it makes the daily habit easier, because the shoes are waiting. You can stop short of a perfect chart, because a rough rating on scrap paper is enough. What counts is that you looked at many actions before you chose one. Run the sort on a single wish this week, and do not try to fix your whole life in one sitting. The rest of the habit work gets easier once the action itself is right.

So back to the wish to feel healthier. The action worth turning into a habit is not the one you grabbed first, and it is not the one that sounds the most heroic. It is one that came out of a long list. Motivation will come and go, and that is fine, because a habit like this does not need it. Sort first, then pick the action that works and that you want.

examples.title: The boot camp sign-up at the shop counter
examples.scenario: Emeka works the front counter at a bike repair shop and wants to feel less drained by closing time. After a rough Friday he is full of drive, and the sign-up page for a five a.m. boot camp is open on his phone. His thumb hovers over the pay button, and he has to decide what to do first.
examples.whatToDo: Close the page and list many small actions for feeling less drained. Rate each on how well it works and how much you want it, then pick the best.
examples.whyItMatters: The burst of drive will fade by midweek, but an action he wants and that works can carry on without it.

examples.title: The study vow after a bad quiz
examples.scenario: Amara just got a low mark on a chemistry quiz at community college, and she wants to feel on top of the course. Tonight she is fired up and writing a vow on a sticky note to study three hours every night. Her pen is still on the note as she decides what to do.
examples.whatToDo: Tear off the vow and list many small study actions instead, such as ten practice questions after dinner. Rate them, then pick one that works and that you want.
examples.whyItMatters: A vow written in a hot moment needs that heat every night, but a small action she likes can survive tired evenings.

examples.title: Four ideas for staying close to a daughter
examples.scenario: Ines wants to stay close to her teenage daughter. She listed four ideas and rated them. A nightly heart-to-heart would work well, but Ines dreads it, so it rates low on wanting. The Tuesday ride to dance class rates well on both. Her sister insists a nightly talk is what good parents do, and Ines holds her pen over the list.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the Tuesday ride, because it works and she wants it, and let it become the habit.
examples.whyItMatters: A habit she dreads would need a wave of drive every night, but a ride she enjoys can keep going on a tired week.

questions.prompt: You want to spend less money, and after a budget video you feel fired up to cut every café visit, takeout meal and subscription starting tomorrow. What do you do?
choices: Vow to cut every one of them tomorrow and push through while you feel fired up.
List many ways to spend less, then pick one that works and that you want.
Choose the single change that would save the most money, and commit to it every day.
questions.explanation: Listing many options and picking one that works and that you want gives a habit that does not need a mood. Pushing through leans on drive that fades, and the biggest saver may be one you dread.

questions.prompt: Idris wants to feel stronger. After a fired-up talk from a friend, he pays for a year of boxing classes and plans to go six days a week. By the third week he has stopped going. What belief led him wrong?
choices: Believing boxing is too hard a sport to turn into a habit.
Believing he should have waited a month before buying anything.
Believing the drive he felt on day one would carry him.
questions.explanation: The trap is trusting a burst of drive to last, but motivation rises and falls in waves. Boxing was not the problem; he never listed other actions or checked what he wanted.

questions.prompt: A teacher wants to feel calmer. She lists many small calming actions, rates them, and picks a two-minute stretch after lunch that she enjoys. What most likely happens during a rough week?
choices: She keeps the stretch on rough days, because it works and she likes it.
She drops it in a busy week, because every habit needs fresh drive each day.
She keeps it only on days she feels motivated, because liking it changes little.
questions.explanation: An action that works and that she wants does not depend on a wave of motivation, so it survives rough days. Habits that need fresh drive each day fade when the mood drops.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm so pumped! I'm going to write for two hours every night until I'm a novelist!" What is your best reply?
choices: Great, ride that energy and push through the tired nights, because it will pay off.
First list other ways to grow as a writer, then pick one you want.
Cut it to one hour a night, so the same plan feels smaller and easier.
questions.explanation: Listing other options first lets your friend find an action that works and that they want. Pushing through leans on drive that fades, and shrinking the same plan keeps the first idea without testing it.

questions.prompt: A parent wants more calm at home. They list many small actions, rate each one, and pick a short tea break after bedtime. Weeks later it still happens. Why did this work?
choices: Because they pushed through the dull evenings with far more willpower than before.
Because any short action turns into a habit, no matter which one gets picked.
Because it works and they want it, so no drive is needed.
questions.explanation: Picking an action that works and that you want means it does not rest on a wave of motivation. Willpower fades, and not every short action fits, so the sorting step is what made it last.

questions.prompt: A wave of motivation hits you on a Sunday, and you suddenly want to eat better all week. What do you do with the wave?
choices: Use it on a one-time job, like clearing a fridge shelf for fresh food.
Promise to cook every single meal from scratch all week, for as long as the energy lasts.
Ignore it completely, since motivation is never worth using for anything at all.
questions.explanation: A wave is best spent on a hard task you do once, because it makes the later habit easier. A big daily vow leans on drive that fades, and ignoring the wave wastes a chance.

questions.prompt: Omar wants better sleep. He lists many actions, rates each for how well it works, and picks the top scorer: no screens after six p.m., which he dreads. He quits within weeks. What went wrong?
choices: He should have written fewer ideas down so the chart stayed simple.
He ignored how much he wanted to do the action he chose.
He should have chosen by gut feeling and skipped the rating step.
questions.explanation: Golden Behaviors need both: the action works and you want it. He used only the first rating, so the choice needed a wave of drive every evening. A long list was not the problem.

reviewCards.front: You want to be a better listener at home. Feeling eager, you are about to promise yourself an hour of quiet talk with your partner every night.
reviewCards.back: List several small listening actions, rate each one, and pick one that works and that you want, because a promise built on eagerness fades when the mood drops.

reviewCards.front: Why is a habit built on a burst of motivation likely to fail?
reviewCards.back: Because motivation rises and falls in waves, so on the day it drops, the habit has nothing left holding it up.

reviewCards.front: Finish the sentence: An action that works, that you want to do, and that you can do is called a ...
reviewCards.back: ... Golden Behavior, and it is the kind of action worth turning into a habit, because it does not need a wave of drive to keep going.

reviewCards.front: Someone wanted to save money, picked the biggest-saving idea on their list, hated it, and gave up within weeks. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: They rated only how well it works and skipped how much they wanted it, so it needed constant drive. A good pick works and is also wanted.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do with a big goal like feeling healthier, and why?
reviewCards.back: List many small actions that serve it, rate each on how well it works and how much you want it, and pick one that scores well on both, because motivation fades and cannot carry a habit.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Turn one big wish into a long list of small actions, rate each, and pick one that works and that you want.

ifThenPlans.context: When a friend across the table says, "You have to try this routine, it changed my life"
ifThenPlans.plan: then I say thanks, write the routine on my list as one idea among many, and rate it that night before trying it.

ifThenPlans.context: When I walk into my kitchen on a Saturday morning feeling a sudden surge of drive to change my life
ifThenPlans.plan: then I spend it on one hard one-time job for my chosen action, like clearing a shelf or buying the gear, and I make no daily vow.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take your list of actions and give each a score from one to five for how well it works and another for how much you want it. Circle the one that scores high on both.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, pick one wish and run the full sort: list many actions, rate each on both scores, and choose one that works and that you want. If a wave of drive arrives, spend it on a one-time setup job.

chapters.title: Shrink the Habit Until It Feels Almost Silly
chapters.hook: Your habit keeps slipping because it asks too much, not because you lack willpower. Think of the one you keep promising yourself, like stretching or reading. Cutting it down until it feels silly is what finally makes it stick.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a big result calls for the full habit and hard pushing. Actually, a habit that feels almost silly in size works better, because a tiny version is easy to repeat, and what you repeat can grow without force.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit keeps slipping, shrink it to a version so small it feels almost silly, and do only that.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one habit you keep missing and cut it to a move so small it feels silly, like touching your toes once. Do only that tonight before bed, because a tiny step is easy to repeat.

memorableLines.text: Shrink the habit until it feels silly, and it stops slipping.

breakdown.fastRead:
A habit you keep missing is usually not too small. It is too big. The fix is to make it smaller than feels reasonable, so small that it feels a little silly. That sounds backward, because most of us believe a big result needs the full habit and hard pushing. But drive does not stay, so a habit that depends on it will fail sooner or later.

BJ Fogg wanted to floss, but he kept missing days. So he made a much smaller promise: he would floss just one tooth. The effort was so small that he kept doing it. Once the one-tooth habit was steady, it grew into flossing his whole mouth. A tiny version is easy to repeat, so it can grow without force. His flossing shows the point, because the full habit kept slipping while the tiny one held. To find what to shrink, Fogg says to ask what is making the habit hard. Then check time, money, physical effort, mental effort, and fit with your routine, because the weakest of those decides. Fix it with skill, a tool, or a tiny version.

Fogg does not say this, but if a habit already runs smoothly, you may not need to shrink it. So back to the habit you keep dropping. Cut it down until it feels almost silly, do only that, and let the repeating do the growing.

breakdown.fullRead:
A habit you keep missing is usually not too small. It is too big. The fix is to make it smaller than feels reasonable, so small that it feels a little silly. That sounds backward, because most of us believe a big result needs the full habit and a lot of hard pushing. But think of how many big habits you started with great energy and dropped within a few weeks. The one you keep promising yourself is probably in that pile.

The big start feels right for good reasons. Big results do take real work, and starting hard feels serious and brave. When you are full of drive, a long workout or an hour of study is easy to promise. The trouble is that drive does not stay, so a habit that depends on it will fail sooner or later. Some days you are tired, busy or in a bad mood. On those days the full habit asks for the most when you have the least. So you miss a day, then another, and you begin to think you are the problem. Really, the habit was too heavy for an ordinary day.

BJ Fogg ran into this with flossing. He wanted to floss, but he kept missing days. So he made a much smaller promise: he would floss just one tooth. One tooth was the whole promise, and doing it was enough. The effort was so small that there was no good reason to skip it, so he kept doing it, day after day.

Then something changed. Once the one-tooth habit was steady, it grew into flossing his whole mouth. He did not force it. A tiny version is easy to repeat, so it can grow without force. The habit became steady first, and only then did it grow. That is why a tiny habit is not a joke or a way of quitting. It is the way in.

Fogg also gives a way to find what to shrink. Ask yourself what is making this habit hard to do. He calls this the Discovery Question, and it points you at the real trouble instead of at your character. Then check five things that can make any habit hard. They are the time it takes, the money it costs, the physical effort, the mental effort, and how well it fits your routine. He calls these five the Ability Chain, because the weakest link decides how easy the habit really is. Say you want to read before bed. If the book is in another room, that is physical effort. If it is a heavy topic, that is mental effort. If it eats up a lot of your evening, that is time. Any one of these can be the weak link.

Then you fix the weak link in one of three ways. You can build skill, so the task gets easier to do. You can get a tool or resource, so something else carries part of the load. Or you can shrink the habit to a tiny version, which is the move at the heart of his method. Skill helps when you do not know how, and a tool helps when a thing is missing. Shrinking helps when the habit is simply too much for the day you have. One kind of tiny version is a Starter Step. It is just the very first move of the habit, like putting on your shoes before a run. Flossing one tooth was a tiny version as well, and both cut the effort down to almost nothing.

His flossing shows why this works, because the full habit kept slipping while the one-tooth habit did not. There was nothing in it to dread, so it did not need a good mood to get done. Now think again about the habit you keep missing. The trouble is likely a weak link, not a weak will, and a tiny version takes that link out. Pick the smallest piece that still counts, such as one stretch or one page, and do only that.

Fogg does not say this, but if a habit already runs smoothly, you may not need to shrink it. And when the missing piece is a tool, such as floss you never bought, getting the tool is one of Fogg's three fixes. A tiny habit also does not have to stay tiny once it feels easy, as the flossing did.

So back to the habit you keep dropping. It does not need more force, and it does not need a stronger you. Cut it down until it feels almost silly, do only that, and let the repeating do the growing.

examples.title: The inbox you promised to clear
examples.scenario: Hamid, a bookkeeper, promised himself he would clear his whole inbox before leaving each day. For three weeks he has missed it, because the pile is huge by five o'clock. It is 4:55, the inbox shows ninety-one unread messages, and his coat is already on the chair. He stares at the screen, unsure whether to try the full clear again.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the habit down to answering just one message today, and do only that until it feels easy.
examples.whyItMatters: One message is too small to skip, so the habit gets repeated and can grow on its own.

examples.title: The two-hour study plan
examples.scenario: Jelena, a first-year nursing student, set a plan to study two hours every night after dinner. She has kept it only a couple of nights this month. Tonight her roommate is laughing in the next room, her textbook sits closed on the desk, and two hours feels like a mountain. She has to decide how to start.
examples.whatToDo: Shrink the plan to opening the book and reading one paragraph, and do only that tonight.
examples.whyItMatters: A one-paragraph job feels too small to dodge, so she shows up and the habit can grow.

examples.title: The guitar in the hallway
examples.scenario: Kofi bought a used guitar and promised himself thirty minutes of practice each evening. Most evenings he skips it, because thirty minutes feels like a lot after a long day. Now he is standing in the hallway at 8 p.m., house keys still in hand, looking at the guitar case by the sofa and deciding what to do.
examples.whatToDo: Open the case and play one chord, and do only that tonight.
examples.whyItMatters: One chord is easy to repeat, so the habit holds and can grow without force.

questions.prompt: You want to start running, but every plan for a daily long run has fizzled by the second week. It is Sunday evening and you are planning the week. What do you do?
choices: Plan a longer daily run than before, and promise to push through the hard days.
Plan to step outside in your running shoes each day, and do only that.
Plan three shorter runs a week, each at least thirty minutes long.
questions.explanation: A step so small it feels silly is easy to repeat, so it can grow. A longer daily run leans on hard pushing. Three half-hour runs are smaller, but still heavy.

questions.prompt: A man tries to read more. He sets a goal of fifty pages every night and misses it for a month. Each time, he tells himself he lacks discipline. What is the trap in his thinking?
choices: He blames his willpower, when the trouble is a goal too big for a normal night.
He needs a bigger goal, like a hundred pages, so that missing it would sting enough to push him.
He has not told enough friends about the goal, so nobody is checking in on him each night.
questions.explanation: Missing again and again points to a weak link in the habit, not in you. Fifty pages is too heavy for a tired night, and a bigger goal only adds weight.

questions.prompt: A home cook keeps skipping the nightly wash-up, so she decides to wash just one plate each night and do only that. What most likely happens over the next few weeks?
choices: She gives up within days, because one plate is too small to count as real effort.
She washes one plate forever, because a tiny habit cannot grow beyond its first size.
The plate gets washed easily, and doing more starts to feel natural over time.
questions.explanation: Doing less today makes repeating easy, so more follows on its own. Quitting over a tiny habit assumes only big effort counts. Staying small forever misses how repeating lets a habit grow.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I want to meditate for twenty minutes every morning, but I keep skipping it. I think I just need to push harder." What is your best reply?
choices: Yes, set an earlier alarm and stretch it to thirty minutes, so it feels serious.
Try one minute of quiet breathing, and do only that until it feels easy.
Maybe wait until your life calms down, then start the full twenty minutes again.
questions.explanation: One minute is small enough to repeat, so the habit holds and can grow. Pushing harder leans on drive, which does not last. Waiting for calm still keeps the heavy version.

questions.prompt: Someone starts a tiny habit of doing two squats after brushing their teeth. Weeks later they are doing a full workout. Why did this work?
choices: The squats were easy to repeat, so the habit held and then grew without force.
The tiny start built up a strong feeling of drive, so the bigger workout came from motivation.
Two squats were already a real workout, so the later sessions were only a small bonus.
questions.explanation: Easy repeats make a steady habit, and a steady habit can grow without force. Drive comes and goes, so it did not carry this. Two squats are tiny on purpose, not a full workout.

questions.prompt: You want to stretch each night but keep skipping it. You ask what makes it hard, and the answer is that it feels like too much after a long day. What do you do?
choices: Block out a full thirty minutes every night and stay strict about it, so it feels serious.
Switch to stretching on weekends only, when you have time for the full routine.
Cut it to one stretch before bed, and do only that until it feels easy.
questions.explanation: The weak link is that the habit is too much for a tired night, so shrinking it fixes the link. A strict full routine adds weight. Weekends only keeps the heavy version.

questions.prompt: A woman keeps skipping her daily walk. She finds that her only shoes hurt her feet, so she decides to walk just one minute a day. What is the trap?
choices: She shrank the habit, but the weak link is her shoes, and new ones fix that.
She should walk much farther each day, so she gets used to the pain and toughens up.
She should stop walking altogether until her feet feel better, however many weeks that takes.
questions.explanation: When the missing piece is a tool, getting the tool fixes the weak link faster than shrinking. Walking farther adds more pain. Stopping altogether loses the habit when new shoes would solve it.

reviewCards.front: You keep skipping your plan to journal for twenty minutes before bed. It is 10 p.m. and your notebook sits on the shelf.
reviewCards.back: Shrink it to writing one sentence, and do only that, because a tiny version is easy to repeat and can grow on its own.

reviewCards.front: Why does a habit you keep missing often get easier when you cut it to a tiny version?
reviewCards.back: Because a tiny version takes almost no drive, so you can repeat it even on bad days, and what you repeat can grow without force.

reviewCards.front: When a habit keeps slipping, the first thing to ask is ...
reviewCards.back: ... what is making it hard to do, because the real trouble is usually one weak link, such as time, money, effort or fit with your routine, not your character.

reviewCards.front: A man wanted to learn piano, so he set an hour a day. He quit after a week, and now he says he has no discipline.
reviewCards.back: He blamed himself, but the hour was too heavy for an ordinary day. A tiny version, like playing one scale, would have been easy to repeat and could have grown.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do when a habit keeps slipping, and why?
reviewCards.back: Shrink it to a version so small it feels almost silly and do only that, because a tiny version is easy to repeat and can grow without force.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Cut a habit that keeps slipping down to a tiny version, and do only that until it feels easy.

ifThenPlans.context: When my coworker at the next desk says, "Lunch?" and I have not walked yet today
ifThenPlans.plan: then I put on my walking shoes at my desk and walk to the front door, and do only that.

ifThenPlans.context: When I sit on the edge of my bed at night and catch myself thinking, "I'll do it tomorrow"
ifThenPlans.plan: then I do the tiny version right there, such as one stretch or one page, and do only that.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, write the habit you keep missing on a sticky note. Name what makes it hard, write its tiny version beside it, and stick the note on your bathroom mirror.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, do the tiny version once and nothing more. On Sunday, ask what made any missed day hard, and let the habit grow only if it now feels easy.

chapters.title: Write the Recipe: After This, I Will Do That
chapters.hook: The new notebook is still under the mail, and you swore on Sunday you would use it every night. So you tell yourself to try harder and remember. Why does that plan keep failing by Thursday?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a new habit starts with remembering and pushing yourself harder. Actually, a habit starts best when it follows something you already do, because that old routine happens on its own and reminds you without any effort.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Tie a new habit to something you already do by writing: after I do this, I will do that.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one sentence on a card today that starts with after and names a daily routine, such as brushing your teeth. End it with one tiny action and do it tonight, because the routine will remind you.

memorableLines.text: Let something you already do start the habit, so you don't have to.

breakdown.fastRead:
The notebook has sat under a pile of mail since Sunday, and Kasia only just noticed it. She is at the dining table at ten at night, telling herself to try harder and remember. That plan feels right because she truly wants the habit, and wanting seems like enough. But her days are crowded, and nothing in them says now.

BJ Fogg says memory and willpower are weak starters, so something else should do the starting. Fogg writes every habit as a short recipe: after something you already do, you do one tiny new thing. The old routine is called an Anchor, and it works as a prompt, which is a signal that tells you to act now. Fogg's own recipe is two push-ups right after using the bathroom. A bathroom visit happens many times a day, so the habit gets many chances and never depends on remembering. The push-ups stick because the bathroom comes first and does the starting. Your own memory is a weaker prompt, because it slips on a busy day, and so is a note or an alert, because it can be missed or tuned out.

So Kasia can write her own recipe: after I sit down to dinner, I will write one line in my notebook. She eats at that table every day, so dinner does the reminding. For a habit you want to keep, write the recipe and let something you already do start it.

breakdown.fullRead:
The notebook has sat under a pile of mail since Sunday, and Kasia only just noticed it. She is at the dining table at ten at night, tired and a little annoyed, telling herself to try harder and remember. On Sunday she was sure she would write one line about her day every evening. Now it is Thursday, and the plan has died without a fight.

Her plan feels right because it is how most of us think about change. If you want something enough, you will remember it, and if you forget, you did not want it enough. So Kasia feels guilty, and the guilt makes her promise to push harder tomorrow. But this treats memory like a strong muscle, and it is not. At the end of a long day, a plan made on Sunday has to compete with work, messages, dinner and a tired brain. Most of us have seen a new habit run on excitement for a few days and then quietly fade.

Wanting also changes through the week. On Sunday, Kasia felt calm and hopeful, so the habit looked easy. On Thursday she feels worn out, so the same habit looks like one more chore. BJ Fogg's view is that motivation comes and goes, and memory is no better. A plan that needs both to show up at the right moment will fail on the first busy day. The trouble is not Kasia. The trouble is that nothing in her evening tells her it is time.

So Fogg says to stop relying on either one. Fogg writes every habit as a short recipe: after something you already do, you do one tiny new thing. The old routine is called an Anchor, and it works as a prompt, which is a signal that tells you to act now. You do not have to remember the new habit, because the old routine arrives on its own and brings the habit with it. The new behavior goes immediately after the anchor, not later in the evening.

Fogg's own recipe is two push-ups right after using the bathroom. The Anchor was not picked by chance. A bathroom visit happens many times a day, so the push-ups get many chances to happen and to turn into a habit. There is no moment when Fogg has to stop and remember, because the bathroom visit does the remembering. The push-ups stick because of what comes before them, not because of strong will.

Fogg sorts prompts into three kinds. A person prompt relies on something inside you, such as your memory or a body signal. A context prompt is something in your surroundings, like a note on the fridge or an alert on your phone. An action prompt is something you do yourself, and an anchor is one of these. For building habits, Fogg says the action prompt beats the other two. Your memory slips on a busy day, and a note or an alert in your surroundings can be missed or become background. A prompt only works if it shows up every time, and a routine you already do always shows up.

Picking the anchor well matters, and Fogg gives three things to check. First, look at where it happens. The new habit should sit in the same place, so you never carry the plan from room to room. Second, look at how often it happens. A daily habit needs a routine that happens at least daily, because a weekly routine gives it only a few chances. Third, look at what the anchor is for. The new habit should match its purpose, like a kitchen habit after a kitchen routine. Then put the new habit immediately after the anchor, with no gap, so the old routine hands it over.

So Kasia can write her own recipe: after I sit down to dinner, I will write one line in my notebook. She eats dinner every day, and she eats it at the same table where the notebook lives. She slides the notebook out from under the mail and leaves it on the table, and dinner does the reminding. She does not need to feel inspired on Thursday, because sitting down is what starts the habit, not her mood. Even a messy evening includes dinner, so the recipe survives a bad day.

Fogg is firm that the recipe beats good intentions, and a softer note that is not Fogg's advice: for a one-time job, such as booking a dentist visit, a note or an alert is enough, because nothing needs to turn into a habit. You do not need a recipe for every chore on your list. Start with one recipe this week. For a habit you want to keep, write the recipe and let something you already do start it.

examples.title: The closing-time card you keep forgetting
examples.scenario: Tariq runs a small bike repair shop. Each night he wants to jot down tomorrow's first job on a card, so he can start fast. For two weeks he has promised himself he will remember, and each morning the card is blank. Tonight he reaches for the sign on the door, ready to flip it to Closed, and has to decide how to make this stick.
examples.whatToDo: Write: "After I flip the sign to Closed, I will write tomorrow's first job on the card by the door." Keep a pen there.
examples.whyItMatters: Closing happens every night, so the sign starts the habit and he no longer has to remember.

examples.title: The homework you never write down
examples.scenario: Jun keeps losing track of homework. Every day he swears he will write each assignment in his planner, and every night the page is blank. Right now the last bell of the day is about to ring, and he has a hand on his locker door. He is about to promise himself again, but he knows how that has gone.
examples.whatToDo: Make a recipe: "After I shut my locker, I will write one assignment in my planner." Say it out loud once.
examples.whyItMatters: Shutting the locker happens every school day, so it reminds him better than any promise.

examples.title: The weekly text to your brother
examples.scenario: Odalys keeps meaning to text her brother once a week, since they live in different cities. Every Sunday she thinks she will do it later, and by Wednesday the week has swallowed it. It is Sunday night now. She is standing at the curb with her hand on the trash bin, her phone in her pocket, and has to decide how to make the text happen.
examples.whatToDo: Write: "After I roll the bins to the curb, I will text my brother one line." A weekly habit needs a weekly routine to follow.
examples.whyItMatters: The bins go out once a week, the same as the text, so the chore does the reminding.

questions.prompt: You want to clear one thing off your desk before leaving work each day, but you keep forgetting. You already shut your laptop every evening. What do you do?
choices: Promise yourself you will remember to tidy up, and push harder on every day you miss.
Write: "After I shut my laptop, I will clear one thing off my desk."
Set a loud phone alert for five o'clock and tidy up whenever it rings.
questions.explanation: The recipe ties tidying to shutting your laptop, which happens every evening, so the laptop starts it. Pushing harder leans on memory, and an alert is easy to ignore.

questions.prompt: A friend wants to move a little money into savings each week. Their plan is to remember on their own and make themselves do it, even when busy. After a month they have done it twice. What is the trap?
choices: Nothing in their week starts the saving, so it depends on memory and mood.
They did not want it enough, so they should feel guilty and try much harder.
They did not ask a friend to nag them, and nagging is the strongest fix there is.
questions.explanation: The plan has no starter, so memory and mood carry it, and they fail on busy weeks. Guilt adds pressure, not a starter. A friend's nagging is a weaker start than something you already do.

questions.prompt: You write, "After I hang my coat at work, I will fill my water bottle." You hang your coat every workday. What most likely happens over the next few weeks?
choices: The habit fades by Friday, because mornings are too busy for anything new.
The habit works only on days you feel motivated, since the coat is just a coat.
The habit gets many chances to happen, because hanging your coat starts it each day.
questions.explanation: A daily routine starts the habit without memory or mood, so it gets a chance every day. Needing motivation is the old idea, and expecting it to fade ignores that the coat does the reminding.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'll do two squats a day. I'll just put it on my to-do list and be strict with myself." What is your best reply?
choices: Being strict works best, so add a penalty each time you miss a day.
Try a recipe: after you brush your teeth, do two squats right away.
Move the list to your phone lock screen so you see it all day.
questions.explanation: Brushing teeth happens daily, so it starts the squats without memory. A to-do list or lock screen is a note, which fades, and penalties add pressure, not a starter.

questions.prompt: A new parent writes, "After I put the baby down for a nap, I will drink a glass of water," and does it every day. Why does this work?
choices: The nap happens daily on its own, so it starts the habit for them.
Parents are very motivated about their own health, so almost any plan would have worked.
Writing it down makes the promise feel serious, so they force themselves to follow it.
questions.explanation: Something already in the day does the starting, so the habit follows it without memory. Motivation and willpower are weak starters, and writing the plan only helps because of the routine it is tied to.

questions.prompt: You want a daily habit of three slow breaths at home. You are choosing what to tie it to. What do you do?
choices: Skip the tie-in, and trust your drive to remember three slow breaths every single day of the week.
Tie it to a team meeting at work that only happens twice a month.
Tie it to taking off your shoes as you walk in the door at home.
questions.explanation: Taking off your shoes happens daily and in the same place as the habit, so it fits. A twice-a-month meeting is too rare for a daily habit, and trusting your drive is the memory-and-willpower plan.

questions.prompt: A coworker wants to thank one teammate every day. They write, "After I refill the office printer paper, I will send a thank-you." The printer is refilled about once a week. What is the trap?
choices: They lack the willpower, so they should push harder after every missed day.
The printer gets refilled rarely, but they want the habit to happen daily.
They should have set a daily alert, since an alert is the strongest kind of prompt.
questions.explanation: A daily habit needs a routine that happens at least daily. The printer gives it only a few chances a month. Pushing harder is the old plan, and an alert is weaker than a routine.

reviewCards.front: You want to note one thing you learned each workday. You already log off your computer every evening.
reviewCards.back: Write a recipe: after I log off, I will note one thing I learned. Logging off happens daily, so it starts the habit for you.

reviewCards.front: Why is "After I pour my coffee" a stronger starter for a habit than "I'll remember in the morning"?
reviewCards.back: Because pouring coffee happens on its own every day and brings the habit with it, while memory and mood come and go.

chapters.title: Feel Good Right Away to Make a Habit Stick
chapters.hook: You and a friend both finish the same tiny habit. You grin the second you're done; your friend saves a big treat for tonight. Whose habit is more likely to stick?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a reward counts whenever it comes, so a treat tonight will do. Actually, the good feeling must land right after you finish, because that is the moment your brain ties it to what you just did.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Celebrate within a moment of finishing, not later in the day, so the feeling sticks to the action.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one small thing you will do today, like clearing a paper off a table, and the second it is done, smile and say 'Yes!' in your head. The feeling sticks to what you just did.

memorableLines.text: Feel the win in the first second, not at the end of the day.

breakdown.fullRead:
You and a friend both finish the same tiny habit this morning. You grin the second you're done, and your friend saves a big treat for tonight. Whose habit is more likely to stick? Most people would bet on the treat, because a big prize sounds stronger than a quick smile. BJ Fogg says that bet is wrong.

The bet feels right because of how the rest of life works. You get paid at the end of the month, and dessert comes after dinner. So a reward seems to count whenever it shows up, and the treat idea sounds like plain common sense. Another idea sits beside it, which is that doing something again and again builds a habit all by itself. You have probably done things many times and still had to talk yourself into them every time. Nothing good was tied to those rounds. Fogg says repeating does not make a habit. Feeling something about it does.

His fix is a move he calls Celebration, which means you deliberately make yourself feel good right after you finish the tiny behavior. A fist pump works, and so does a smile or a quiet 'Yes!' It takes only a second or two, and it can be as small as a nod. The gesture is not the point. The point is the feeling, a quick flash of knowing you did it and did it well. You are not bragging to anyone, only telling yourself the truth. Fogg calls that feeling Shine, and he says Shine is what wires the habit into you.

Timing matters because of how your brain links things. It ties a good feeling to whatever you did in the moment before. If the feeling comes in the first second after you finish, it sticks to the habit. If it comes at nine at night, it sticks to the couch or the dessert, and the morning habit is long forgotten. A late treat belongs to the whole day, so it blurs together everything you did. Your brain has no way to tell which small action earned it. So Fogg tells people to celebrate the instant they finish, not at the end of the day or the week.

Think of Celebration as a feeling you can make on demand. Motivation comes and goes, so you cannot count on it showing up. But you can give yourself a small good feeling in one second, every time. A feeling needs no tools and costs nothing, so you can make one anywhere. Fogg links it to a guiding rule of his, which is to help people feel successful. A habit you finish with a glow is one you want to do again. A habit you finish with a shrug is one you must push yourself to repeat. Over time the habit starts to feel good, and that carries it through days when you do not feel like it.

Run the opening again with this in mind. Your friend does the habit, waits all day, and eats the treat at night. The treat is nice, but the good feeling gets tied to the evening, not to the habit. You did the habit and grinned right away, so the good feeling got tied to the habit itself. A late treat cannot do this job however big it is, because timing comes first. A quick feeling that is real and strong works best. The next time the same moment comes around, your habit already has a little warmth attached to it.

What you pick has to feel real to you. A big cheer that makes you roll your eyes will not make you feel successful, so it will not wire anything in. Try a few and keep the one that gives you an honest lift. A fist pump, a word under your breath, or a smile in the mirror can all do it. Then use it the instant you finish, every time, even after the smallest win. At first it may feel silly to cheer for something so small. That is normal, and it passes once the good feeling starts to come easily. Do not wait until you feel like it.

Fogg is firm that the feeling must come right away, and nothing that comes later takes its place. You can keep it small and quiet, because a private smile still counts if it feels real. In a meeting or on a train, a silent 'good' to yourself is enough. The celebration that counts most is the one right after you finish, though Fogg also encourages a good feeling when you remember the habit and while you do it. A softer note that is not Fogg's advice: a treat tonight can be a nice extra, but it does none of the work.

Both of you did the work, but only one of you told your brain about it in time. Waiting for tonight makes a habit feel like a chore you get paid for later. Celebrating now makes it feel like something you just won. If you want a habit to hold, feel good in the first second after you finish, not tonight.

examples.title: The note you wrote at closing time
examples.scenario: Rafael is a line cook who started a tiny habit of writing one prep note on the kitchen whiteboard before he leaves. Tonight he caps the marker at 11:40, tired and ready to go. He has told himself he will buy a nice pastry on Sunday as his reward. His ride is honking outside, and he has one second to decide what to do.
examples.whatToDo: Pump a fist or whisper 'Nice' the second the marker is capped, then head out. Enjoy the Sunday pastry as a bonus.
examples.whyItMatters: The good feeling lands on the note he just wrote, not on a pastry days later, so the habit itself gets the credit.

examples.title: One math problem on the bus
examples.scenario: Hye-jin, a high school junior, wants to do one math problem the moment she sits down on the bus home. Today she finishes it just as the bus pulls out. She has promised herself a movie on Friday if she keeps this up all week. The pencil is still in her hand, the bus is bumping along, and she wonders what to do next.
examples.whatToDo: Give a small nod and a quiet 'Got it' right as the pencil lifts. Let Friday's movie be a bonus.
examples.whyItMatters: Her brain ties the good feeling to the problem she just solved, so the habit starts to pull her.

examples.title: A glass of water in the driveway
examples.scenario: Mateus parks in the driveway after work, and the glass of water in his cup holder is his new tiny habit. He just finished it. He plans to save his reward for Saturday, a fancy coffee. His phone is lit up with messages, his thumb hovers over it, and he has to choose what to do first.
examples.whatToDo: Smile and say 'Yes' about the water before picking up the phone. Treat the Saturday coffee as an extra.
examples.whyItMatters: The feeling attaches to the water he just finished, while Saturday's coffee would only attach to the coffee.

questions.prompt: You just finished a tiny habit: refilling the bird feeder on your balcony at 7 a.m. You are about to head inside for a shower. What do you do?

Smile and say 'Yes!' right there, before you walk back inside.
Think about how well it went once you are standing in the shower.

Nothing is wrong, because a good feeling counts whenever it arrives.
A stretch this small is not big enough to deserve any real pride.

questions.prompt: A student does one flashcard at a desk each evening and feels nothing when done, then moves on, planning a long bath on Sunday. What most likely happens to the habit?

Skip any reward at all and let willpower carry the habit.

chapters.title: Let a Tiny Habit Grow Without Raising the Goal
chapters.hook: Raising your goal is the quickest way to wreck a habit that finally works. You do your small thing every day, it feels easy, and you decide it is time to ask more of yourself.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think an easy habit should get a bigger daily goal. Actually, keep the small version as your only promise and treat extra as a bonus, because a bigger minimum needs more motivation each day, and motivation comes and goes.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do the tiny version every time, and treat anything extra as a bonus, never as the new minimum.
chapters.tryThisNow: Do your tiny habit at its usual moment today, and do more only if you feel like it. Tomorrow's promise stays just as small, so a bad day cannot break it.

memorableLines.text: Keep your promise small, and let anything extra be a bonus.

breakdown.fastRead:
Do not raise the goal on a habit that feels easy, because that is often when it starts to die. Wanjiru has sketched one small thing at her dining table each evening, right after she clears the plates. Tonight it felt so easy that she wants to promise a full page every night. That sounds sensible, because at school and at work, doing well meant a higher target.

BJ Fogg grew his push-up habit the other way. He started with two push-ups at one set moment in his day. When he felt like doing more, he did more, but he never made more the new minimum. Over time two at a time became many each day. His reason is that a bigger minimum needs more motivation every day, and motivation comes and goes. Two push-ups still get done on a bad day, so the habit survives. His habit grew because the floor stayed tiny, not because he lifted it. Habits also spread, because each small win builds your skill at changing.

So Wanjiru keeps tonight's promise at one small sketch. If she feels like filling a page, she can, but tomorrow's promise is still one small sketch. You can stop short of this advice when a deadline or a doctor's plan fixes the amount, because then that amount is your floor. Otherwise, make the small version your whole promise, and count anything beyond it as a gift.

Wanjiru has sketched one small thing at her dining table each evening, right after she clears the plates. It takes almost no time, and she has not missed a night. Tonight it felt so easy that she wants to promise herself a full page every night from now on. She is proud of herself, and she thinks raising the goal is the grown-up thing to do.

Her plan feels right because everything else in life taught her that progress means raising the bar. A runner adds miles, a student takes harder classes, and a worker is handed bigger targets. So when something starts to feel easy, it seems like a sign that you are ready for more. Staying at the same small size even feels a little lazy, as if she were cheating. But a habit is not a school course or a training plan, and it works in a different way.

Look at what the bigger promise asks of her. A full page needs more time, more energy and more will than one small sketch. On an evening when she gets home late and tired, that promise looks heavy, and she may skip it. Then she has broken her own word, and the habit starts to feel like something she fails at. One missed night turns into two, and the sketchbook goes back on the shelf. The goal went up on a good day, but it had to be met on every day, including the bad ones.

BJ Fogg grew his own push-up habit the other way. He began with two push-ups at one set moment in his day. Two is a number so small that it is hard to argue with, so there was nothing to put off or dread. He did them every time that moment came, and that was the whole promise. Anyone could keep that promise on a calm day or a stressful one. That is exactly why it was worth starting at the size where it could not fail.

Then the habit grew, and the way it grew matters. When Fogg felt like doing more, he did more. On those days he let himself keep going and enjoy it. But he never turned that extra into a new minimum, so the next day's promise was still two. Little by little, two at a time became many each day. The growth came from wanting to, not from a demand he set for himself. Extra was a bonus every time, and a bonus cannot be missed.

His reason is simple. A bigger minimum asks for more motivation every day, and motivation comes and goes. Some days you feel full of energy, and other days you feel flat. If the promise depends on feeling strong, it breaks on the flat days. A tiny floor needs almost no motivation, so it still gets done when you are tired, busy or in a bad mood. Because the floor holds, the habit survives, and a habit that survives has time to grow. His push-ups got big because the floor stayed tiny, not because he kept lifting it.

A habit grows in two ways, and both come from starting tiny. The first is the one you can see, when the behavior itself gets larger, like more push-ups at a time. The second is quieter, because one habit can spread into others. Each time you keep a tiny promise, you build skill at changing and faith that you can do it. That faith carries over, so the next habit you try starts from a better place. You do not need to force either kind of growth. You only need to keep succeeding at the small size, and the success does the pushing.

So Wanjiru keeps tonight's promise at one small sketch. If she feels like filling a page, she can, and she should enjoy it. Tomorrow evening, after the plates are cleared, the promise is still one small sketch. If she is worn out, she sketches her mug in a few quick lines and calls it done. That counts as a full success, because the promise was never about the page. The extra pages will come on the evenings when she wants them, and the other evenings will keep the habit alive.

Wanting to do more is a good sign, and you can follow it freely. It just must never turn into a debt you owe tomorrow. You can stop short of this advice when a deadline or a doctor's plan fixes the amount, because then that amount is your floor. Most habits people want, such as sketching, moving more or tidying up, are not like that. For those, make the small version your whole promise, and count anything beyond it as a gift.

examples.title: The headset log that feels too small

A coworker says real pros write a full paragraph. Nadir opens the log before his first call, thinks about the paragraph, and has to decide what his promise is from now on.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the promise at one line, and write the paragraph only on days he feels like it, treating it as a bonus.
examples.whyItMatters: A one-line floor still gets done on a rough shift, so the log survives while paragraphs can grow on good days.

examples.title: Three flashcards versus thirty
examples.scenario: Ngozi has study hall every afternoon. When she sits down, she flips through three vocabulary cards, and she has done it for weeks. Her friend laughs that three is a joke and tells her to promise thirty a day. Ngozi holds the deck and has to decide what her promise is.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the promise at three cards, and go through more only when she feels like it, with no pressure to repeat it tomorrow.
examples.whyItMatters: Three cards survive a draining day, while thirty becomes a debt that she may skip, and skipping feels like failing.

examples.title: Two easy laps on a great morning
examples.scenario: Sora pulls on their swim cap at the pool every morning and swims two easy laps, which they have done for a month. Today the water felt great and they had energy left. Standing at the edge, they think about making four laps the daily minimum. They have to choose the promise.
examples.whatToDo: Swim the extra laps today if they want, but tell themself tomorrow's promise is still two easy laps.
examples.whyItMatters: Today's good energy is not guaranteed tomorrow, so a two-lap floor keeps the habit alive on a groggy morning.

questions.prompt: You drink one glass of water each time you sit down at your desk, and it has felt easy for weeks. Today you feel great. What do you do?
choices: Raise the promise to four glasses a day, since one glass has become too easy to count.
Drink one glass, drink more if you like, and keep tomorrow's promise at one glass.
Drink one glass now, then raise the promise after one more week of perfect days.
questions.explanation: Extra water is a bonus, so the promise stays at one glass. Raising it now makes tomorrow's promise bigger, and waiting a week to raise it still turns extra into the new minimum.

questions.prompt: A man plays two minutes of piano scales after dinner and loves it. He tells himself he will make it twenty minutes every night. What belief leads him wrong?
choices: Believing that two minutes of scales is too short to count as real practice.
Believing that right after dinner is a poor time of day to practice.
Believing that when a habit feels easy, the daily promise ought to grow.
questions.explanation: He treats easy as a signal to raise the minimum, but a bigger promise needs more motivation, and that comes and goes. Thinking two minutes is too short is a different mistake.

questions.prompt: A woman sweeps her porch for one minute each evening when she gets home. Some evenings she cleans the whole porch, but she counts one minute as a full day. What most likely happens over the coming months?
choices: She keeps the habit through busy weeks, and longer cleaning days slowly become common.
She stays stuck at one minute, because a promise that never grows cannot lead to more.
She keeps the habit, but the extra cleaning stops, because nothing makes her do it.
questions.explanation: The one-minute floor holds on bad days, and the bonus cleaning happens when she feels like it, so the habit grows by itself. Staying stuck is the fear behind raising the goal.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My two-minute tidy-up is easy now, so I'm making it half an hour every day." What is your best reply?
choices: Good plan, since a bigger number keeps you moving forward and shows you are serious.
Keep the two minutes as your promise, and do more on the days you want to.
Try half an hour for now, then drop back to two minutes if it gets too hard.
questions.explanation: Two minutes stays the floor and extra becomes a bonus, so it survives bad days. Starting at half an hour and dropping back later still sets a big minimum first.

questions.prompt: A cyclist promises herself one block of riding after dinner. On many nights she rides ten. A year later, the habit is still going. Why does this work?
choices: A one-block promise needs little motivation, so it still gets done on low-energy nights.
A bigger target each week keeps the rider pushing, because more is asked every single night.
The ten-block nights do all the real work, and the one-block promise hardly matters at all.
questions.explanation: A tiny floor asks little of you, so it survives tired nights, and the extra comes when you want it. Raising the target each week asks for more motivation, which comes and goes.

questions.prompt: You have texted one friend every Sunday evening after dinner for two months, and it feels natural. Now you feel guilty that it is only one text. What do you do?
choices: Promise yourself three calls a week, since one text no longer feels like enough.
Keep the one text as the promise this month, then raise it to three calls next month.
Keep one text as the promise, and call on the evenings when you really feel like it.
questions.explanation: A call on a good evening is a bonus, so the promise stays at one text. Raising it later, even on a schedule, still turns extra into a new minimum.

questions.prompt: A man who walked five minutes every day raised his goal to forty after two weeks. Then he missed four days in a row and felt like a failure. What belief led him wrong?
choices: Believing that five minutes was never worth walking, so he should have started higher.
Believing that once five minutes felt easy, the new minimum should jump to forty.
Believing that missing four days is a sign a person cannot build any habits.
questions.explanation: He turned an easy habit into a heavy minimum, so a bad stretch broke it. Starting higher would only have made the same weight arrive sooner.
