reviewCards.back: Keep three breaths as the promise and take more only when you want to, because a bigger minimum needs more motivation, and motivation comes and goes.

reviewCards.front: Why can a tiny promise survive a terrible day when a bigger one often does not?
reviewCards.back: A tiny promise needs almost no motivation, so you can still meet it when you are tired or stressed. A bigger one needs more drive, and drive comes and goes.

reviewCards.front: When a habit feels easy and you want to do more, treat the extra as ...
reviewCards.back: ... a bonus, never the new minimum, because tomorrow's promise stays at the tiny size that always gets done.

reviewCards.front: Someone did a one-minute plank each morning for a month, then promised five minutes every morning. By week two they had quit and felt like a failure. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: They made the extra the new minimum. Five minutes needs more motivation than a bad morning can give, so they missed, and the miss felt like failing. One minute as the promise, with more by choice, would have saved it.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how should you let a tiny habit grow?
reviewCards.back: Keep doing the tiny version every time, do more only when you feel like it, and never turn that extra into tomorrow's minimum.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Keep the tiny version as your whole promise, and let anything extra stay a bonus you do only when you want to.

ifThenPlans.context: When my coworker at the next desk says, "Only that? You could easily do more," about my tiny habit
ifThenPlans.plan: then I answer that the promise stays tiny, and I do extra only if I feel like it that day.

ifThenPlans.context: When I stand at the bathroom sink after my tiny habit and think, "I should do more tomorrow"
ifThenPlans.plan: then I say out loud that tomorrow's promise is the same tiny size, and I do extra now only if I want it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, open the notes app on your phone and write your habit's tiny size in one line. Add the words extra is a bonus under it, and read it the next time you feel like raising your goal.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each day this week, make a tick once the tiny version is done, whatever extra you did or skipped. At the end of the week, check that your promise is still the same tiny size.

chapters.title: Remove the Cue Before You Fight the Urge
chapters.hook: The candy bowl sits two feet from your keyboard, and it is three o'clock again. You say no once, then twice, and then your hand is already unwrapping one. What if the nudge never came at all?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a bad habit stops once their willpower is strong enough to say no each time. Actually, you stop it faster by removing what sets it off, because a nudge you never feel costs no willpower at all.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick one small piece of a bad habit and remove what sets it off before anything else.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick the one snack or app you grab most at work, and put it out of sight before your next break today. A nudge you never see costs you no willpower, so there is no fight.

memorableLines.text: Do not fight the urge; take away the thing that starts it.

breakdown.fastRead:
The candy bowl on the front desk sits two feet from Rohan's keyboard, and it is three o'clock again. He tells himself no and holds out for a while. Then he gets tired, and a wrapper is in his hand. BJ Fogg says not to wrestle the whole habit at once. Split it into small, specific behaviors, such as candy from the bowl, soda from the machine and cookies after dinner. Pick the easiest one. Then use the three levers from starting a habit, but in this order. First take away the cue, the thing that sets the behavior off. Next make it harder to do. Only last try to want it less. Rohan's easiest piece is the bowl, so he moves it to a back cupboard and sets clementines on the desk instead.

At three o'clock the desk is bare, so Rohan has nothing to say no to. This works because he cleared the nudge once instead of fighting it again and again. You can stop short of clearing your whole home, because some cues, like a phone your job needs, cannot go; for those, make the habit harder. So the way out is not a stronger no. Take away what sets off one small piece of a bad habit.

breakdown.fullRead:
The candy bowl on the front desk sits two feet from Rohan's keyboard, and it is three o'clock again. He tells himself no and holds out for a while. Then a patient is late, the phone rings twice, he gets tired, and a wrapper is in his hand. He promises himself that tomorrow will be different, and he is sure the problem is that he does not have enough willpower.

That belief feels true because quitting looks like saying no. We have all watched someone turn down dessert and called it strength. Rohan can even win on some days, so it seems that winning more often is all he needs. A bad habit also feels like a flaw in who you are, and a flaw seems to call for a stronger you. So he keeps trying harder at saying no, and he feels guilty each time it fails.

But the plan has a hole in it. Every no is a fresh fight, and the bowl is still there for the next one. Willpower rises and falls from moment to moment, so Rohan cannot count on it being there at three o'clock. The bowl never changes, because it just sits and waits. In a long day he has to win every single time, and the bowl only has to win once. A plan that needs a perfect record every day is a plan built to fail.

BJ Fogg says to stop wrestling the whole habit at once. Snacking is not one thing, so do not treat it as one. Break it into small, specific behaviors, such as candy from the bowl, soda from the vending machine and cookies after dinner. Each one has its own nudge, its own time of day and its own fix. Then pick the easiest one to change first. Starting with the easiest one matters, because an early win shows you that the method works and gives you the nerve for the harder pieces. For Rohan, that is the bowl, because it is the simplest to deal with and it happens at the same spot every day.

Next comes the order, and the order matters. You use the same three levers you use to start a habit, but this time you pull them in a set order. First, take away the cue. A cue is the nudge that starts a behavior, such as a snack in sight, a buzzing phone or a certain time of day. If the nudge never comes, the behavior often never starts. Second, make the behavior harder to do. Put the thing on a high shelf, delete the app or add steps. Last, and only if you must, try to want it less. Fogg puts this one at the end because wanting rises and falls without warning, so it is the least reliable lever. The cue and the effort are things you can change in a minute, with your hands.

So Rohan starts with the cue. He moves the bowl to the back cupboard, where he cannot see it from his chair. The desk is now bare at three o'clock, so nothing sets off his hand. Then he adds a swap. He puts a bowl of clementines where the candy used to be, so his hand has something new to do in the spot where the old habit lived. An empty spot pulls the old habit back, and a new small habit fills it. None of this takes a single no, because he made one choice ahead of time and the choice keeps working while he is busy. By the next week the cupboard can be just a cupboard, and three o'clock can be just a time.

Suppose the bowl is gone, but the three o'clock urge now walks Rohan to the vending machine. That is a different behavior with its own nudge, so he treats it the same way. He cannot hide a machine in the hall, so he uses the second lever and leaves his coins at home, which makes the snack harder to get. And if nothing works at all, Fogg says to scale the change back instead of pushing harder. Pick a smaller piece and start again. A small change you finish beats a large one you drop.

Fogg is blunt here: he does not want you leaning on willpower at all, because it is the tool most likely to give out. The cue is the first thing to try, and it often costs almost nothing. You can stop short of clearing every cue from your home, because one removed cue is enough to start and some cues, like a phone your job needs, cannot go. For those, use the second lever and make the habit harder. Do not wait to feel ready, because the move takes a minute and needs no good mood. You do it once, ahead of time, and it keeps working after you stop thinking about it.

So think of Rohan at three o'clock. The desk is bare, the clementines are in sight, and there is no fight to win. He did not become a stronger person overnight. He just stopped asking his willpower to beat a bowl that never gets tired. The way out was never a harder no. Pick one small piece of a bad habit, take away what sets it off, and do that before anything else.

examples.title: The 10:30 pastry run
examples.scenario: Bao wants to stop spending money on pastries at work. Every morning at 10:30, his coworker Dana leans into his cubicle and says, "Pastry run?" and he is up and walking before he thinks. It is 10:28 on Monday, and he has just spotted Dana getting up from her desk, keys in hand. He has about a minute to decide.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Dana before 10:30 that you are skipping the pastry run this week, so her usual question never reaches you.
examples.whyItMatters: Without Dana's question, there is no nudge to say no to, so Bao spends no willpower at all.

examples.title: The video tab that waits for you
examples.scenario: Tobias keeps losing his homework hours to a video site. Every evening he opens his laptop, and the site waits in a pinned tab at the top of his browser, right beside his class page. He tells himself he will watch one clip. It is 7 p.m., the laptop is open, and his cursor is hovering over the pinned tab.
examples.whatToDo: Unpin and close the tab, then delete the bookmark, so the site no longer sits in front of him every time he opens the laptop.
examples.whyItMatters: He removes the cue once, so each evening starts without a pull he has to resist.

examples.title: The tablet on the sofa arm
examples.scenario: Mikael wants his evenings back from scrolling. His tablet lives on the arm of the sofa, so he picks it up the moment he sits down after dinner. Tonight he is carrying his plate to the sink, and the tablet is still on the sofa, waiting for him to come back. He has a few seconds to decide where it goes.
examples.whatToDo: Put the tablet on its charger in the hallway drawer now, and set a crossword book on the sofa arm where it used to sit.
examples.whyItMatters: With the tablet out of reach, sitting down no longer starts the scrolling, and the crossword gives his hands a new job.

questions.prompt: You answer work email all weekend, and the red badge on your phone's home screen pulls you in. You want your Saturdays back. What do you do?
choices: Turn off the badge and move the email app off your home screen.
Keep the badge on and say no to the email each time you feel the pull.
Remind yourself each morning that work email is not worth your Saturday.
questions.explanation: The badge is the cue, so removing it once costs no willpower. Saying no each time means a fresh fight every time. Telling yourself to care less is the last lever, not the first.

questions.prompt: A student wants to stop eating chips at her desk, so she leaves the bag in plain view and says no harder each day. By Friday the bag is empty. What belief led her wrong?
choices: Believing she should have started by wanting chips a lot less.
Believing a firm no can beat a bag that stays in plain view.
Believing a smaller bag would have solved it on its own.
questions.explanation: A bag in view keeps the cue running, so every no is a new fight. Wanting chips less is the last lever, and a smaller bag would still sit in view.

questions.prompt: A driver always checks texts at red lights. Today, before starting the car, they put the phone in the glove box. What most likely happens at the next red light?
choices: They still reach for it, because urges always win at red lights.
They spend every red light fighting the urge, using up willpower.
The urge barely shows up, because nothing in sight sets it off.
questions.explanation: The phone was the cue, and out of sight it cannot set off the urge. Thinking urges always win, or that it takes constant fighting, ignores what happens when the nudge is missing.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'll stop buying things online by just resisting. The store app sends sale alerts all day, and I'll ignore every one." What is your best reply?
choices: Good plan, ignoring every alert will build the strength you need.
Try thinking about the savings, so you want the sales less.
Turn off the sale alerts first, so the nudge never arrives.
questions.explanation: Alerts are the cue, so turning them off once removes the fight. Ignoring each one leans on willpower, and wanting sales less is the weakest lever to start with.

questions.prompt: Someone who ate ice cream from the freezer every night stopped buying it. Within days the late-night urge nearly disappeared. Why did this work?
choices: With none in the house, nothing set the habit off, so there was no fight.
Skipping the purchase built their willpower until it grew strong enough to refuse.
They stopped caring about ice cream, so the habit faded away on its own.
questions.explanation: Removing the cue meant the habit never started, so no willpower was spent. Building strength is not what happened, and losing the wish is the last and least reliable lever.

questions.prompt: You drink soda from a machine at lunch, at dinner and in the car. You want to cut back this week. What do you do?
choices: Ban soda in every place, and say no to it each time it shows up.
Start with the lunch machine, and walk a route that skips it.
Start with dinner soda, since it is the one you enjoy the most.
questions.explanation: Split the habit, start with the easiest piece, and remove its cue by changing your route. Banning everything leans on willpower, and the piece you enjoy most is the hardest to start with.

questions.prompt: A man wants to stop checking his phone while his kids play at the park. He reads about why phones harm families so he will want it less, but keeps the phone in his hand. It fails. What is the trap?
choices: Starting with the weakest lever and leaving the cue in view.
Choosing the park, since one short moment is too small to change.
Reading anything, since facts cannot change how people act.
questions.explanation: Wanting it less is the last lever, and it fails while the phone stays in view. Take away the cue first, by putting the phone in a bag out of reach.

reviewCards.front: Your watch lights up with a news alert during every meeting, and you check it each time. You want to stop. What is your first move?
reviewCards.back: Switch off that app's alerts. Without the nudge, the habit has nothing to start it, and you spend no willpower.

reviewCards.front: Why is removing a cue better than saying no to the urge each time?
reviewCards.back: Removing it takes one choice ahead of time, but saying no is a fresh fight every time, and willpower runs thin as the day goes on.

reviewCards.front: To stop a behavior, pull the levers in this order: first take away the cue, then make it harder to do, and last ...
reviewCards.back: ... try to want it less, because wanting comes and goes, so it is the least reliable lever.

reviewCards.front: A woman wants to quit late snacks, phone in bed and soda all at once. By day four she has dropped all three. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She took on the whole tangle together. Split the habit into small behaviors, start with the easiest one, and remove its cue first.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do first when you want to stop a bad habit, and why?
reviewCards.back: Pick one small piece of the habit and remove what sets it off, because a nudge you never feel costs no willpower.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Take away what sets off one small piece of a habit, so you never have to fight the urge.

ifThenPlans.context: When I unpack the groceries on Sunday evening and pick up the box of cookies
ifThenPlans.plan: then I put it on the top shelf of the hall closet, not in the kitchen, and set the fruit bowl on the counter instead.

ifThenPlans.context: When my phone lights up with a shopping banner that says "Flash sale ends tonight"
ifThenPlans.plan: then I press and hold the banner and turn off notifications for that app before I tap anything else.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, write three small behaviors that make up one habit you want to stop. Circle the easiest, write down what sets it off, and take that one thing away before you go to bed.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday, check how last week's removed cue went. If the urge is gone, pick the next small behavior and remove its cue. If it is not, make the first one harder to do, or scale back, before you push harder.

chapters.title: Help Others Change by Designing, Not Lecturing
chapters.hook: You have explained, calmly and more than once, why the shared habit matters, and everyone agrees with you. Still nothing changes at home or at work. If lecturing doesn't change the people around you, what does?
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think they must explain why it matters and keep pushing until their family or team changes. Actually, you get further by making one shared habit easy and rewarding for them, because people repeat what feels good, not what they are told.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick one shared habit, then make it wanted, easy, prompted and rewarding for others instead of lecturing them.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person at home or work today what they would enjoy doing more together, and write down their answer, because a habit they already want is the easiest one to shape.

memorableLines.text: Don't lecture people into a habit; make it easy, wanted and worth repeating.

breakdown.fastRead:
Umar has explained three times this month why packing school bags the night before would save his family's mornings. Everyone nods, yet every morning still ends in a hunt for shoes. So what is missing, if everyone already agrees? Umar thinks understanding changes people, so he adds more reasons and a louder voice. That feels right because a good reason can move you, but the push fades before a tired family reaches the door.

Fogg says the steps you use on your own habits also work for families, teams and communities. He points to a family and to a hospital staff. In both, the move is to pick one shared behavior and shape it, so the change comes from design, not pressure. Find what the others already want, and make the behavior easy. Add a prompt, which is a signal that tells them to start. Then help them feel successful right after. Fogg says these steps are for helping people do what they already want, never for pushing them into what they don't.

His family already wants calmer mornings, so Umar picks bags by the door and adds hooks to make it easy. The click of the dishwasher door is the prompt, and a cheer when a bag goes on its hook feels good. You can stop short of banning all talk, since asking what people want is a fine start. What changes people is one shared habit built so they want it, can do it easily, get a nudge and feel good after.

breakdown.fullRead:
Umar has explained three times this month why packing school bags the night before would save his family's mornings. Each time, his partner and both kids nodded and said it made sense. Yet every morning still ends in a hunt for one missing shoe and a shout down the hallway. So what is missing, if everyone already agrees with him? Umar has an answer ready. He thinks they just need to hear it more clearly, and maybe a little louder.

This belief feels true because it has worked on you before. When you finally see why something matters, you feel a pull to act. So you assume others will feel the same pull once you explain it well. Lecturing also feels like doing something. After a long talk, you feel you have tried, so the next step must be theirs. But the pull from a good reason is a mood, and moods pass. Fogg is blunt about this: motivation is not something you can count on. A speech may lift the room for an evening, and then the morning rush arrives.

There is a second problem. The people around you usually already know what you want from them. Umar's family can repeat his reasons back to him word for word. So another round of reasons gives them nothing new, and it can start to sound like blame. Nobody likes feeling like the problem in their own home or workplace. That is why the talking often makes the habit feel heavier instead of lighter. The family nods to end the talk, not because anything in the morning has changed.

Fogg's answer is to stop pushing and start designing. He says you do not need a second method for groups. The steps you use on your own habits also work for families, teams and whole communities. He gives a family and a hospital staff as cases. In both, the move is the same: pick one shared behavior and shape it, instead of pressuring people into it. His core idea is to help people do what they already want to do, and to help them feel successful. Keep it to one behavior.

The first move is to find what the others already want. Umar can find this out by asking instead of telling. Umar does not need his family to care about his reasons. His daughter wants to stop being rushed, and his partner wants to leave the house without a fight. A habit that serves those wishes already has a pull behind it, so Umar does not have to supply the pull with speeches. Teams work the same way: a crew that wants shorter meetings will take to a habit that gets them out sooner. If the habit serves nothing they want, no clever design will rescue it.

The second move is to make the behavior easy for them. Packing a bag at night is a chore when the bag lives at the bottom of a closet. Umar puts a row of hooks by the front door, so the bag has an obvious home and packing takes almost no effort. The third move is a prompt, which is a signal that tells people to start so nobody has to remember. The click of the dishwasher door closing works, because it happens every night anyway. A good prompt does the reminding, which means Umar no longer has to.

The fourth move is to help them feel successful. Right after a person does the behavior, a small good feeling is what makes them want to do it again. So when a bag goes on its hook, Umar gives a cheerful thank-you, or the family trades a quick high five. It should feel warm, not like a grade, and a speech wrapped around the thank-you would spoil it. This is where lecturing does worst, because a lecture brings the bad feeling before the behavior and none after. A design puts the good feeling right where the habit happens.

Fogg treats the ethics of changing others as part of the method. These steps are for helping people do what they already want to do. They are not for tricking or forcing people into what they do not want. If Umar's family truly does not want calmer mornings, design cannot fix that, and he should drop the plan. You can stop short of banning all talk, because one honest question about what people want is a fine place to begin.

So Umar puts away the speech. He asks what the family wants, picks bags by the door, adds hooks, lets the dishwasher click do the reminding, and cheers each bag. Nobody has to be talked into anything, because the habit now fits the way they already live. The puzzle at the start has a plain answer. What changes people is one shared habit built so they want it, can do it easily, get a nudge and feel good after.

examples.title: The fridge full of unlabeled containers
examples.scenario: Dmitri runs a small restaurant kitchen, and unlabeled containers keep piling up in the walk-in fridge. He has lectured about waste at three staff meetings, and every cook agreed. Tonight the cooks are grumbling about a slow closing shift. Before service, he stands at the pass with a roll of tape and a marker, and a fourth speech already half formed in his head.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the speech. Hang the tape by the fridge door, since the cooks want a faster close, and thank the first one who labels.
examples.whyItMatters: The cooks already want a quicker close, so easy tape at the right spot and a thank-you beat a fourth speech.

examples.title: The workshop after every meeting
examples.scenario: Wren captains her school's robotics club, and the workshop is a mess after every meeting. She has scolded the team twice, and each time they said sorry. Everyone keeps saying they want to stop wasting time hunting for tools. Now the meeting is ending, backpacks are zipping, and Wren takes a breath to give a third scolding.
examples.whatToDo: Swallow the scolding. Draw an outline for each tool on the pegboard, play one song as the cleanup signal, and thank whoever finishes first.
examples.whyItMatters: Outlines make the habit easy, the song starts it, and the thank-you feels good, so a team that wants less hunting can follow.

examples.title: The empty dog bowl at seven
examples.scenario: Elif shares a flat with two roommates and a dog. The bowl was empty again at seven, and nobody knew who fed him last. Elif already sent a long message about responsibility, and both roommates replied with a thumbs-up. They adore the dog. Now she stands at the empty bowl with a second message half typed.
examples.whatToDo: Skip message two. Leave the scoop on the bowl as the prompt, add a tick chart beside it, and cheer whoever ticks first.
examples.whyItMatters: Both roommates already love the dog, so a visible scoop and a happy cheer make feeding easy and fun, which a message could not.

questions.prompt: You organize a weekly running club. Everyone says they want to start on time, but half the group still shows up late. What do you do?
choices: Send the whole group a long message on why being on time really matters.
Meet closer to everyone's homes and cheer whoever arrives first.
Ask each runner to promise to be on time from now on, no matter what.
questions.explanation: Meeting closer makes arriving easy, and a cheer feels good, so a group that already wants to start on time can do it. A long message and promises both lean on reasons and memory.

questions.prompt: A manager wants the team to take real lunch breaks. At three meetings, the manager repeats facts about burnout, yet nothing changes. What is the trap here?
choices: Leaning on facts, when nothing in the day makes a break easy or rewarding.
Not repeating the facts often enough, so people forget why breaks really matter.
Choosing a habit so large that the team cannot even begin to do it.
questions.explanation: The manager is leaning on facts and repeats. People who already know breaks help still skip them, so the day needs a design that makes a break easy and feels good. Repeating louder does not fix that.

questions.prompt: A parent wants the family to keep wet shoes off the living room rug, which everyone says they want. The parent sets a bench with a basket at the door and thanks warmly anyone who uses it. What most likely happens?
choices: The family ignores the bench, because a basket cannot replace a good talk.
The family uses it only while the parent stands there to watch them.
More of the family uses it, since it is easy and the thanks feels good.
questions.explanation: The bench makes the step easy, and the thanks makes it feel good, so people repeat it. Nobody needs a lecture or a watching parent, because the setup does the work.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My team never updates the shared task board, so I'll keep reminding everyone in meetings why it matters." What is your best reply?
choices: Keep going, since hearing the reason enough times will make it stick for them.
Ask what they want from it, then make updating quick and thank them.
Track who updates the board and name the slow ones in each meeting.
questions.explanation: Asking finds what they want, and a quick update with a thank-you makes the habit easy and rewarding. Repeating the reason is only pushing, and naming slow people adds pressure instead of design.

questions.prompt: A volunteer group wants more people at its Saturday clean-up. Instead of a speech, the lead puts a sign-up sheet by the coffee urn and thanks each person who adds a name. Sign-ups rise. Why does this work?
choices: People sign up once the sheet gives them enough good reasons to want to join.
Everyone can see who has not signed, so the pressure makes people join.
Members who already want to help meet an easy step and a warm thanks.
questions.explanation: People who already want to help only needed an easy step in a spot where they gather and a thanks that felt good. Pressure and extra reasons were never what moved them.

questions.prompt: You want your department to recycle more. Staff say they care, but the only bin is at the far end of a long hallway. You have a few minutes at the next meeting. What do you do?
choices: Put a bin at the end of each desk row and thank the first users.
Spend the meeting on the reasons recycling matters for the planet.
Ask everyone to carry recycling to the far bin every Friday afternoon.
questions.explanation: A bin within reach makes recycling easy, and a thank-you makes it feel good, so staff who already care will do it. Speeches and a Friday trek only push.

questions.prompt: A coach wants every player to stretch after practice. Most players say they dislike it and want to leave early. The coach plans a snack table, a playlist and loud cheers to push stretching anyway. What is the trap?
choices: Making stretching so easy that the players will not take it seriously at all.
Designing around a habit nobody wants, instead of asking what players want.
Skipping a long talk about why stretching matters before the snack table opens.
questions.explanation: These tools are for helping people do what they already want. If players do not want the habit, snacks and cheers become pressure, so the coach should first ask what the players want.

reviewCards.front: Your family says it wants to cook together on Sundays, but it never happens. What do you do this week?
reviewCards.back: Pick that one shared habit and shape it: set out the pans the day before, give it a clear start signal, and cheer when it happens, because shaping beats nagging.

reviewCards.front: Why does a longer speech about a shared habit usually fail with a team?
reviewCards.back: Because reasons lift motivation only for a short while, and people often already know them. An easy, prompted, rewarding habit keeps working after the mood is gone.

reviewCards.front: Before you design a habit for a group, the first thing to find out is ...
reviewCards.back: ... what the others already want, because these methods help people do what they want and can never fairly force them into what they refuse.

reviewCards.front: A dad hung a chore chart and checked it daily with a stern face. The kids stopped looking at it within weeks. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He pushed with pressure and a bad feeling instead of designing. The chores were not easy, nothing prompted them, and nobody felt good after, so no pull was left once the stern face went away.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'design, don't lecture' ask you to do with a family or team?
reviewCards.back: Pick one habit the others already want, make it easy, give it a clear prompt, and help them feel good right after, instead of explaining and pushing.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Shape one shared habit so the others want it, find it easy, get a prompt and feel good, instead of pushing them with reasons.

ifThenPlans.context: When someone in the car says, 'We should really do that more'
ifThenPlans.plan: then I ask what they would enjoy about it, pick one shared habit from the answer, and name one thing I can make easier by tonight.

ifThenPlans.context: When I hear myself starting 'How many times do I have to tell you' with anyone at home or work
ifThenPlans.plan: then I stop, ask what would make the habit easier for them, and fix one small thing in the room instead of finishing the sentence.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: By tomorrow night, turn that answer into one shared habit and change one thing in the room so it is easy, then thank the first person who does it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Keep the one shared habit going for seven days. Each time someone does it, give a quick thank-you in the moment and drop any lecture. If nobody seems to want it by midweek, ask again and switch to a habit they do want.
